findings.finding: Insights: After i rounds each 2^i score pattern appears 2^{20‑i} times; after 20 rounds all 2^{20} binary win‑patterns are unique, giving distinct scores. Pairings must match equal‑score groups; a winner must be faster than its paired loser. Thus each round splits a group into a “fast half” (winners) and “slow half” (losers) via a perfect matching where every winner is paired with a slower runner. The set of possible winner subsets of size half are exactly the *upward‑closed* subsets of the group’s total order (any faster runner can be a winner only if a slower one exists to lose). Consequently the tournament’s final ranking corresponds to a linear extension of a poset defined by these constraints. Counting N reduces to counting linear extensions of the Boolean lattice of rank 20, i.e., N = (2^{20})! / ∏_{k=0}^{20} (2^{k}!)^{\binom{20}{k}}. Compute v₂(N) and v₅(N); k = min(v₂,v₅). Take k mod 10⁵. (Pitfall: ensure the “upward‑closed” condition, not any half‑subset.)

Insights: Final scores are 20‑bit binary strings; each round splits each equal‑score group into winners (bit 1) and losers (bit 0). Within a group of size 2m we must partition into L,R (|L|=|R|=m) admitting a perfect matching where every l∈L is slower than its paired r∈R. This holds iff, after sorting the group, the i‑th smallest element of L is slower than the i‑th smallest of R for all i (dominance condition). Thus a ranking (bijection runner↔binary code) is valid iff for every node of the binary tree, the set of runners assigned to its left subtree is “dominated” by the set assigned to its right subtree. Counting such labelings yields N; compute its 10‑adic valuation k and output k mod 10⁵.

Insights: After 20 rounds each runner gets a unique 20‑bit score, so final ranking is a permutation of 2²⁰ numbers. Pairings are arbitrary within equal‑score groups, each round adds a bit (1 to faster, 0 to slower). Thus a permutation is realizable iff there exists a sequence of 20 perfect matchings where in each matching the “1‑bit” side is always faster than the “0‑bit” side. This is equivalent to constructing a 20‑level binary decision tree whose leaves are the runners, with the rule that at each internal node the left child (bit 1) must consist of faster runners than the right child (bit 0). Count such labelings → number of linear extensions of the poset formed by the complete binary tree of height 20 where each node imposes “all left‑descendants > all right‑descendants”. This poset is the product of a chain of length 20 and an antichain of size 2²⁰, giving N = (2²⁰)! / ∏_{i=0}^{19} (2^{20-i})! . Compute k = ν₁₀(N) = Σ_{p=2,5} Σ_{j≥1} ⌊(2²⁰)/p^j⌋ – Σ_{i=0}^{19} Σ_{j≥1} ⌊(2^{20-i})/p^j⌋. Evaluate modulo 10⁵. (Pitfall: ensure scores are distinct → no ties.)

Insights: After 20 rounds each runner’s score is a unique 20‑bit binary number; the fastest always gets 111…1, slowest 000…0. Possible final rankings = linear extensions of the poset defined by “if a faster runner can be forced to lose a round to a slower one, then the slower may outrank the faster”. This poset is exactly the Boolean lattice of subsets of {1,…,20}: each runner corresponds to a binary vector of wins; a runner can outrank another iff his vector is not component‑wise ≤ the other’s. Thus N = number of linear extensions of the 20‑dimensional Boolean lattice. Compute v₂(N) and v₅(N) via known formulas (e.g., Stanley’s hook‑length product for the lattice). Then k = min(v₂(N),v₅(N)) mod 10⁵. (Pitfall: assuming all permutations possible; actually only extensions of this poset.)

Insights: After n=20 rounds each group halves, giving every runner a unique 20‑bit win vector. In a score‑equal group of size 2k, any subset of k can be winners iff each winner can be paired with a slower loser → Hall’s condition ⇒ winners must be a “lower set” in the speed order (if a runner wins, all faster in the group also win). Thus each round forces the set of winners to be an initial segment of the group’s speed ranking. Consequently the tournament’s final ordering corresponds to a binary tree where at each node the left subtree (winners) consists of the faster half of its players. Hence the final ranking is exactly any permutation obtainable by recursively splitting each set into a faster half and slower half. Number of possible orderings N = product over all internal nodes of (choose size/2 from size) = ∏_{k=0}^{2^{20}-1} C(2^{⌊log₂(k)⌋+1},2^{⌊log₂(k)⌋}) = ∏_{i=0}^{19} (C(2^{i+1},2^{i}))^{2^{20-i-1}}. Compute v₂(N) and v₅(N) via Legendre’s formula on each binomial, sum exponents, then k = min(v₂,v₅). Finally output k mod 10⁵.

Insights: Final scores are unique 20‑bit numbers; ranking = permutation of players. At each round i, each group of size 2^{21‑i} must split into exactly half winners. Winners must be matchable with slower losers ⇒ selection of winners must satisfy ballot condition (prefix wins ≤ losses). Number of valid winner subsets per group = Catalan C_{2^{20‑i}}. Total possible rankings N = product over i=1..20 of (C_{2^{20‑i}})^{2^{i‑1}}. Compute k = ν_{10}(N) = ν_2(N)+ν_5(N). Use ν_p(C_n)=ν_p((2n)!)-2ν_p(n!); apply Legendre. Sum contributions for p=2,5 across i. Finally k mod 10^5 is answer.

Insights: Final scores are 20‑bit strings; faster runner must have lexicographically larger string. Thus any tournament yields a non‑increasing sequence of binary strings (by speed). Feasible strings are exactly those where each round’s winners can be matched with slower losers ⇒ Catalan condition: scanning speeds from slowest to fastest, at any prefix #wins ≤ #losses. Hence the multiset of scores corresponds to a Dyck path of length 2·2^20. Number of possible orderings = Σ over all Dyck words of product of factorials of block sizes (identical scores). Compute exponent of 10 in this sum → k. Pitfalls: assuming arbitrary winner sets; must enforce matching condition (Catalan). Use generating functions or known formula for Σ (multinomial·product factorial) = (2·2^20)!/(2^20)! . Then k = v_10((2·2^20)!)-v_10((2^20)!). Take mod 10^5.

Insights: Final scores = 20‑bit win vectors; ranking = descending binary order. Pairings each round split each equal‑score group into pairs; the faster in each pair gets a 1. Thus winners must be exactly the faster half of each group (any set of size ½ works, since we can match each chosen winner with a slower loser). Hence after each round each group is forced to keep its top half as 1‑bit carriers. Consequently the set of achievable win‑vector assignments equals all permutations where, for every prefix length k, the players with a 1 in the k‑th bit are precisely the top half of those sharing the first k‑1 bits. This yields N = ∏_{i=0}^{2^{20}−1} (binomial coefficient constraints) → N = ∏_{j=0}^{19} ( (2^{20−j})! / ( (2^{19−j})! )^2 ). Compute v₂(N), v₅(N) via Legendre; k = min(v₂,v₅); output k mod 100 000.

Insights: After each round groups split into winners/losers; a winner set in a group of size 2n is any “Dyck” subset → Catalan Cₙ possibilities. For 2²⁰ runners, N = ∏_{j=0}^{19} C_{2^{j}}^{2^{19‑j}}.  

v₂(C_{2^{j}})=1 (j≥1), so v₂(N)=2¹⁹‑1=524 287.  

v₅(C_{2^{j}})= carries₅(2^{j}+2^{j}) – v₅(2^{j}+1). Compute for j=0…19 → values [0,0,0,1,1,0,2,1,0,1,1,3,3,4,0,2,3,5,4,6].  

v₅(N)=∑2^{19‑j}·v₅(C_{2^{j}})=121 818.  

k = min(v₂,v₅)=121 818; k mod 10⁵ = **21 818**.  

Pitfalls: assume scores become distinct (true after 20 rounds); use Catalan count for winner subsets; compute v₅ via carries (Kummer).

Insights: Final scores are distinct 20‑bit numbers. At each round a group of size 2t splits into winners/losers; feasible splits = Catalanₜ (Dyck paths).  
N = ∏_{k=0}^{19} Catalan_{2^{k}}^{2^{19‑k}}.  
v₂(C_{2^{k}})=1 (k≥1), v₅(C_{2^{k}}) computed via Legendre.  
v₂(N)=Σ_{k=1}^{19}2^{19‑k}=2^{19}‑1=524 287.  
v₅(N)=Σ_{k=0}^{19}v₅(C_{2^{k}})·2^{19‑k}=121 818.  
k = min(v₂,v₅)=121 818 → k mod 10⁵ = **21 818**.  

Pitfalls: assume scores distinct (they are); count splits via Catalan, not permutations. Use Legendre for prime exponents.

Insights: Final scores are binary strings of length 20. A node of 2m players splits into m winners/losers; possible winner sets = Catalan Cₘ (Dyck paths). Nodes are independent ⇒  
\(N=\prod_{s=2}^{20}C_{2^{s-1}}^{2^{20-s}}\).

Valuations: \(v_2(C_{2^t})=1\) (since \(\binom{2^{t+1}}{2^t}\) has one 2‑factor, \(2^t+1\) odd).  
\(v_5(C_{2^t})=c_t-v_5(2^t+1)\) where \(c_t\) = carries when adding \(2^t+2^t\) in base 5. Compute for \(t=1..19\):  
\(c_t-v_5(2^t+1)=[0,0,1,1,0,2,1,0,1,1,3,3,4,0,2,3,5,4,6]\).

Thus  
\(v_2(N)=\sum_{s=2}^{20}2^{20-s}=2^{19}-1=524287\).  
\(v_5(N)=\sum_{t=1}^{19}2^{19-t}(c_t-v_5(2^t+1))=121818\).

\(k=\min(v_2,v_5)=121818\).  
\(k\bmod10^5=21818\).  

Pitfalls: ensure Catalan count per node, independence of nodes, and use carries (Kummer) for \(v_5\).
